pl-l4d15c2-d1e112.summary: Lists five ways scourges come: to increase the merits of the just through patience, as Job; to guard virtue lest pride tempt, as Paul; to correct sins, as Miriam's leprosy; for God's glory, as the man born blind; or as the beginning of punishment, as Herod, showing here what follows in hell. So Nahum's authority does not compel us to think all things punished temporally will not be punished further by God.
claims: Scourges serve merit, protection, correction, God's glory, or initial punishment.
Temporal punishment does not always exclude eternal.

pl-l4d15c2.summary: Explains five purposes of scourges: increasing the merits of the just through patience (Job), guarding virtue against pride (Paul), correcting sin (Miriam's leprosy), the glory of God (the man born blind), and the beginning of punishment (Herod), showing here what follows in hell. So Nahum's text does not require that all punished temporally will not be punished further.
claims: Temporal punishment can be the beginning of eternal punishment.
Not all punished temporally escape further punishment.
